A week ago it came to light that UC Berkeley math professor Zvezdelina Stankova, who went viral in an August 15th essay deploring the poor preparedness of some of her students, actually used AI for her essay.

> The article was flagged by the AI detector Pangram as 33% AI-generated or AI-assisted writing. A similar result was found in a June open letter from STEM faculty advocating for standardized testing. “The faculty team and a number of journalists worked intensively on my draft over a period of three weeks with multiple drafts, meetings,” Stankova said in an email. She added that she used AI to help edit the piece but that the article is the result of “several hundred person-hours of intensive human work and deliberation, of which about 80 hours are my own.”

Her argument still stands. I think it does detract a bit from her credibility. Here, she’s taking a moral high ground, when that ground is soft. If you want to use AI, fine, but accusing others of being lazy or unprepared, whilst using AI and having an editorial team, is a bit rich. But it is true that columnists, even for one-off op-ed pieces, have a large staff of uncredited editors–including AI assistance–despite their sole name being on the byline.

Conversely, students are expected to have minimal outside help, and when they avail themselves of such tools or assistance, it’s called being lazy, cheating, or being unprepared. This seems wrong. But that isn’t the point of this post. The question is, “why do so many people, professionals and students alike, depend so much on AI for writing?” It’s well known that AI writing is easy to spot (even without Pangram) and worse, yet people still use it.

But not to only pick on her, billionaire and legendary investor Stanley Druckenmiller admitted that he used AI to help write an August column for the Wall Street Journal , generating widespread criticism and a tepid defense from the paper, which nonetheless stood by the essay. So apparently writing what is effectivity a high school assignment is harder than being one of the most successful money managers in the world.

The most obvious explanation for the proliferation of AI-assisted writing is to save time. It’s simply easier to outsource the writing to AI. Even if AI-assisted writing is obvious and worse, this is a tradeoff that is preferable to no writing . So if given a choice between AI help and less or no writing, the former is a compromise that strikes a balance between the need to communicate and the reader lowering his or her expectations.

Math and computer science have tons of collaboration. It’s not uncommon for a math paper to have more than a single author, whereas writing is more of a solitary endeavor. Or STEM professors will delegate work to graduate students, such as proofreading. When you delegate writing, you’re no longer a writer; it’s something else. Even if the ideas are yours, it’s implicitly assumed when you read something, that the author actually wrote it.

AI is not merely a tool in the same way that a hammer is used to build a house. With AI, the authorship itself is uncredited, making it closer to ghostwriting, whereas the analogue of a hammer for writing would be, say, a pencil, but it’s not like the pencil is doing the writing. This is why AI writing is so controversial, because it breaks the trust between the reader and the author. Indeed, people feel like they are being ripped off when they see AI writing and it’s undisclosed.

A second, less explored explanation is that writing itself is hard. Linguists in the 20th century, such as Pinker and Chomsky, argued that language is innate. But this is only speech. Writing and reading involve decoding and encoding printed language, and there is nothing inherently natural about this. This is how you end up with the situation where everyone has verbal fluency, but literary and writing ability are much more unequally distributed. People can spend twenty years reading and writing in school or have doctorates, and still struggle to organize a 1,500-word argument.

Of the thousands of people on twitter or readers in general, only a handful do any long-form writing. Of those who do, output tends to be spotty or infrequent (e.g. the occasional Malcolm Gladwell op-ed). Examples such as David Brooks, Richard Hanania, Noah Smith, and Freddie deBoer, who write long-form on a weekly, consistent basis, are truly anomalous. Literally maybe only dozens of people.

For example, before I write, I may jot down some ideas in unpublished tweets, which I review later, as a sort of outline. Having to rewrite these notes into a full, cogent essay is considerably more work, as it often entails extra effort substantiating these notes–much more so than the idea-generation process. I can understand why someone would either just stick to tweeting, or paste the notes into AI and have it weave them into an essay.

Blaise Pascal (incorrectly attributed to Lincoln) is quoted as saying that he would write a shorter letter if he had more time. I disagree. Even with experience writing, I still sometimes find it hard to overcome the inertia of starting, and then having to arrange my thoughts in a way that is, I hope, cogent and pleasing to the reader. Writing a tweet, or even a series of tweets, is so much easier and faster. It does not scale linearly, so composing 300 words as a series of tweets takes much less time than 300 words in essay form. The popularity of Twitter suggests that others probably find it easier, too.

Essay-style writing, as opposed to tweeting, is about taking a chain of inchoate thoughts and turning them into something that has a self-contained structure. This is an added level of difficulty and orthogonal to the idea-generation process itself, and is in some ways harder, because there are so many wrong ways to do it, resulting in bad writing even if the underlying ideas are sound.

For example, going back to the original example, her essay could be broken or distilled into the following ideas:

-too many incoming freshmen are unprepared for college-level math at UC Berkeley -a certain percentage lack proficiency of even the basics, such as fractions -this is attributable to making the SAT optional, which has backfired -the SAT should be mandatory for admission

These would be perfectly fine as a series of tweets, but not as a standalone essay. That requires: structure, grammar, organization, transitions, style, and some form of narration or storytelling rather than a recitation of facts. I’m sure Mr. Druckenmiller ran into this problem. He probably knew what he wanted to say when distilled into bullet points, but he just couldn’t fill in the other ingredients to turn it into an essay–hence AI. And AI still cannot actually do this, without it sounding like AI. Even for this essay, I still had to run it through AI to find mistakes, which it inevitably did.
